Learning When to Trust Retrieval: A Disagreement-Aware Gate for Few-Shot Inverse Dynamics
Constantin Ertel¹, Phillip Kerger¹
¹ University of California, Berkeley
Preprint draft | Revised 24 October 2026
Abstract
Video-based robot policies increasingly split control in two: a video model predicts the future, and an inverse-dynamics model (IDM) turns that predicted future into actions. When a new task arrives with only five demonstrations, the IDM is the part that must adapt. Retrieving the demonstrations' actions is a natural way to adapt it, and a learned gate can mix them with the IDM's own prediction. Such a gate fails exactly when it matters: if it sees only the robot's state, it keeps trusting a source-trained prediction that is wrong for the new task. We introduce a disagreement-aware gate that also sees how confident the retrieval is and how far the two predictions disagree, and we train it on deliberately corrupted predictions so that it learns when to defer to retrieval. We froze every design choice on LIBERO-Goal and then ran once on 30 sealed tasks from three other LIBERO suites, with three frozen image encoders, five demonstrations per task and three seeds. We find that, without any training on the new task, the gate beats nearest-neighbour regression on all 30 tasks for every encoder (chunk MSE 0.378 vs 0.528 with MAE) and beats the same head without the new inputs (0.378 vs 0.425). We also find where it falls short: encoder fine-tuning reaches lower error at 7 to 17 times the compute per update, and in closed-loop simulation plain nearest-neighbour regression completes the most tasks (44% vs 38%), while lower offline error does not predict success.
Keywords: inverse dynamics; retrieval; gating; few-shot adaptation; robot manipulation; LIBERO.
1. Introduction
Give a robot five demonstrations of a task it has never seen, such as putting a bowl on a plate, and ask it to do the task again from a new start. Systems built on video models approach this in two steps. A generative model predicts what the scene should look like next, and an inverse-dynamics model (IDM) infers the actions that produce that change: frames in, actions out. UniPi introduced this split for text-conditioned video planning [1], and it now appears across recent systems, from visual subgoals in π0.7 [2] and the action modules of GE-Act 2.0 and VPP2 [3],[4] to the separate inverse-dynamics model of Rhoda AI's Direct Video-Action system [5]. When the video model is fixed, adapting to a new task means adapting the IDM, and a new task rarely comes with more than a few demonstrations.
The simplest way to use those demonstrations is to look up the closest recorded moment and copy its actions, as VINN does [6]. A learned head should do better: it can attend over several retrieved candidates and blend them with its own prediction through a gate [7],[8]. In an earlier study, we found that it can also do much worse. Our attention-and-gate head (RAID v7) beat nearest-neighbour regression on average, but on one held-out LIBERO-Goal task its error was 1.7 times that of nearest-neighbour regression (0.682 vs 0.406). Its errors tracked the source-trained prediction (Pearson 0.97 across query demonstrations), not the retrieved actions. The gate saw only the robot's state. It had no way to notice that the source-trained prediction was wrong for this task.
This raises a simple question: when should a learned model trust retrieved actions over its own prediction? Our answer is that the gate making this choice must see when the two disagree. RAID v8 gives the gate two kinds of input it was missing, the confidence of the retrieval and the per-dimension disagreement between the direct prediction and the retrieved prior. The inputs alone are not enough. During source training the direct prediction is rarely far off, so the gate never learns what to do when it is. We therefore corrupt the direct prediction on purpose: for a quarter of the training rows, the mix receives another input's prediction. The gate then trains on exactly the situation it will face on a new task, a direct prediction that disagrees with confident retrieval.
We test this idea with a protocol built for statistical confidence, and we keep design and evaluation apart. Every design choice, including the gate variant, the learning rates and the closed-loop gripper rule, was made on the ten LIBERO-Goal tasks. We then froze the methods, settings, analysis code and three hypotheses in a digest-bound amendment and ran the benchmark once on 30 sealed tasks from three other LIBERO suites [9], with three image encoders: MAE [10], DINOv2 [11] and SigLIP [12]. Every comparison uses paired task-level bootstrap intervals and Holm-corrected tests.
Our contributions:
A disagreement-aware retrieval gate, trained with direct-path corruption. Without target training, it has lower action error than nearest-neighbour regression on all 30 sealed tasks for each of three encoders, and lower error than the same head without the new inputs (Section 6.1). The corruption is essential: on development tasks, the new inputs without it make the head worse, not better (Section 6.2).
A compute-aware comparison with fine-tuning. A head update on frozen features costs 4 to 7 ms; a LoRA or full fine-tuning update costs 52 or 128 ms. The gated head reaches its best error within 25 updates, but encoder fine-tuning reaches lower error with more compute (Section 6.3).
A closed-loop test without a video generator, which replays recorded target frames in the LIBERO simulator. The adapted gated head completes more tasks than head-only fine-tuning, LoRA and full fine-tuning; nearest-neighbour regression still completes the most, and lower offline error does not predict success (Sections 6.4 and 6.5).
